Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

In the austere halls of Harrowhold, Lord Harrow's daughter Elys falls for Garr, a stable-hand; their tender, clandestine love collides with duty and status when a marriage is arranged for Elys. A betrayed plan and an intercepted letter force a cruel choice: order will be upheld at the expense of the two who loved across the divide.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-elys: Elys Harrow: the lord's only daughter, nineteen. Curious and quietly fierce, raised inside Harrowhold; she knows the rules but has never loved any of them.
- char-garr: Garr: a stable-hand/servant in his early twenties. Steady, taciturn, surprisingly gentle and practical; he knows the estate's edges and a few books stolen nights in the clerk's light.
- char-lord-harrow: Lord Harrow: Elys's father, late forties, widower and master of Harrowhold. Stern, status-minded, believes household order is the only safe thing for his line.
- char-marta: Marta: Elys's maid and confidante, thirty, pragmatic and loyal. Knows the household's gossip and the thin places where rules fray; she becomes a reluctant accomplice.
- char-aldric: Aldric of Westbrook: the suitor Lord Harrow selects, mid-twenties, polished and useful to the alliance Harrow wants. Not cruel but not Elys's match; his presence forces the lovers' choices.
- char-rowan: Rowan: captain of the household guard, early thirties. Professional, feels the tension between duty and conscience; carries orders without asking too many questions — at least at first.
- loc-harrowhold: Harrowhold: the lord's manor — stone house with a great hall, a high balcony over the gardens, a walled garden, stables and a paved courtyard. It is both a home and a small, ordered world.
- loc-walled-garden: The walled garden of Harrowhold: a secluded patch of fruit trees, clipped hedges and an old stone bench. The garden is where unequal people can meet unseen if they dare.
- loc-balcony: The west balcony of Elys's chamber: overlooking the gardens, a narrow, sheltered ledge where conversations can be lowered into the night.
- loc-great-hall: The great hall: the center of household life, where proclamations are made, alliances announced and the social choreography of the estate is performed.
- loc-courtyard: The paved courtyard before the servants' door and stables. A gateway between worlds and, in this story's end, the place where order will be publicly enforced.
- obj-hairpin-ivory: An ivory hairpin, carved with a tiny willow motif. Elys's keepsake; it becomes the lovers' token and the object that fuses intimacy to consequence.
- obj-letter-sealed: A folded and sealed note: an earnest, simple message from Garr that will be intercepted. The letter is a practical attempt at arranging escape that becomes evidence.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural elements or anachronistic technology — the story is grounded in a quasi-medieval household world.
- Household law: the lord has the social and legal authority within his household to arrange his heir's marriage and to punish servants for crimes (including conspiracy or aiding escape). Secret tokens or promises carry emotional meaning only; they confer no legal standing.
- Marriage is a legal/sacral act that requires the lord's approval (or a priest with jurisdiction). A clandestine private promise between a noble and a servant does not create a recognized marriage in this world.
- Social mobility is limited: servants cannot inherit land or titles; they can be freed, bound, or punished, but any change to status must be explicitly recorded if it is to be a fact later in the manuscript.
- No deus ex machina: once a scene sets a fact (a letter intercepted, an order given), later scenes must carry its consequences — events are causal and traceable.
- Objects introduced (hairpin, sealed letter) are physical evidence: their existence, who possesses them, and any inscriptions or marks must be recorded in the index if later referenced.

The garden takes them like a secret: a pocket of late light pressed into stone and clipped hedges, apple-sweet air smelling faintly of the stables, the great house above them as solid and unmoving as a law. Elys moves down the gravel path with the careful feet of someone practiced at making no sound. She is nineteen and keeps her life in measures—lessons, needlework, vespers—until the narrow hour after vespers when the house hums and the stables' clatter covers secrets.

He is waiting on the old stone bench beneath her balcony, shoulders squared as if to carry the world on them. Garr smells of tack and hay; the place of him in Harrowhold is a practical one: a stable-hand with a small freedom, the kind that lets a man choose where his hands go and not where his name sits in a ledger.

Marta stands a little back, half in shadow on the path where the hedges meet the wall. She is Elys's maid and confidante—pragmatic, watchful—and tonight she has the face of someone who has decided to be a sentinel rather than a snitch.

Elys sits, folding her hands over her skirts. The hairpin that lives with her, a thin thing of ivory, catches the last light—a willow carved on its length, slim as a reed. She has kept that pin on a low tray at her dressing table since she was a child; it is the sort of small thing a person names by habit and forgets is precious until someone else needs it.

Garr takes her hand without hurry. He watches her fingers, the careful way she lays out her words like stitches. For a moment the world narrows to the dip of her wrist and the pale gleam of the pin.

"Take it," she says, and the sound of her voice is less than a vow but more than a promise. "Take it, Garr."

He closes his hand around the thin ivory and tucks it into the rough of his palm as if expecting to hide something precious beneath skin used to work. The motion is small and final.

Marta's answer is a whisper that the leaves nearly steal. "I'll watch. I won't tell."

They sit with that—three people under a sky that forgets to judge them for the length of a breath. Above them, somewhere in the great hall, dinner is ending. At the head of the table Lord Harrow says little; his silence rearranges the room: the servants walk straighter, voices lower. His power is the architecture of the household, a constant that presses against the edges of gatherings and decisions.

Elys looks at Garr as if testing a truth against the feel of his face. "It is not law between us," she says, the sentence practical, like mending a seam. "We are not wed. We are two people who have found one another where the house said we could not."

He gives a laugh that is almost a breath. "No priest, no ring. I can't give you what the law gives, Elys. But I can give you this."

He stands and draws nearer, the grit of the yard in his boots. "I will come back," he says, and the words are plain as a pledge laid on wood.

"I will wait," she says, as plain and as absolute. The bench between them keeps their knees from touching, and still their bodies make a map of decisions—small, stubborn.

They do not speak of routes or times or foolish dreams. Garr's hands are rough around the ivory; Elys counts the willow's carved leaves the way other people count prayers. Marta lifts her chin, a concession and a guard.

When they part, it is by degrees: Garr slipping away to the stables' shadow, Elys to the narrow balcony that is more a promise than a door. The hairpin is in his palm; the garden keeps its hush. The household resumes its order above them, Lord Harrow's presence folded into the sound of footsteps and the closing of shutters.

On the stone bench the willow's tiny leaves throw a grin of shadow. The promise between them is not a binding; it is a private law they give one another, absolute in the small jurisdiction where they have authority: the hour after vespers, the old stone bench, the willow-pin warm in his hand.

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

The garden takes them like a secret: a pocket of late light pressed into stone and clipped hedges, apple-sweet air smelling faintly of the stables, the great house above them as solid and unmoving as a law. Elys moves down the gravel path with the careful feet of someone practiced at making no sound. She is nineteen and keeps her life in measures—lessons, needlework, vespers—until the narrow hour after vespers when the house hums and the stables' clatter covers secrets.

He is waiting on the old stone bench beneath her balcony, shoulders squared as if to carry the world on them. Garr smells of tack and hay; the place of him in Harrowhold is a practical one: a stable-hand with a small freedom, the kind that lets a man choose where his hands go and not where his name sits in a ledger.

Marta stands a little back, half in shadow on the path where the hedges meet the wall. She is Elys's maid and confidante—pragmatic, watchful—and tonight she has the face of someone who has decided to be a sentinel rather than a snitch.

Elys sits, folding her hands over her skirts. The hairpin that lives with her, a thin thing of ivory, catches the last light—a willow carved on its length, slim as a reed. She has kept that pin on a low tray at her dressing table since she was a child; it is the sort of small thing a person names by habit and forgets is precious until someone else needs it.

Garr takes her hand without hurry. He watches her fingers, the careful way she lays out her words like stitches. For a moment the world narrows to the dip of her wrist and the pale gleam of the pin.

"Take it," she says, and the sound of her voice is less than a vow but more than a promise. "Take it, Garr."

He closes his hand around the thin ivory and tucks it into the rough of his palm as if expecting to hide something precious beneath skin used to work. The motion is small and final.

Marta's answer is a whisper that the leaves nearly steal. "I'll watch. I won't tell."

They sit with that—three people under a sky that forgets to judge them for the length of a breath. Above them, somewhere in the great hall, dinner is ending. At the head of the table Lord Harrow says little; his silence rearranges the room: the servants walk straighter, voices lower. His power is the architecture of the household, a constant that presses against the edges of gatherings and decisions.

Elys looks at Garr as if testing a truth against the feel of his face. "It is not law between us," she says, the sentence practical, like mending a seam. "We are not wed. We are two people who have found one another where the house said we could not."

He gives a laugh that is almost a breath. "No priest, no ring. I can't give you what the law gives, Elys. But I can give you this."

He stands and draws nearer, the grit of the yard in his boots. "I will come back," he says, and the words are plain as a pledge laid on wood.

"I will wait," she says, as plain and as absolute. The bench between them keeps their knees from touching, and still their bodies make a map of decisions—small, stubborn.

They do not speak of routes or times or foolish dreams. Garr's hands are rough around the ivory; Elys counts the willow's carved leaves the way other people count prayers. Marta lifts her chin, a concession and a guard.

When they part, it is by degrees: Garr slipping away to the stables' shadow, Elys to the narrow balcony that is more a promise than a door. The hairpin is in his palm; the garden keeps its hush. The household resumes its order above them, Lord Harrow's presence folded into the sound of footsteps and the closing of shutters.

On the stone bench the willow's tiny leaves throw a grin of shadow. The promise between them is not a binding; it is a private law they give one another, absolute in the small jurisdiction where they have authority: the hour after vespers, the old stone bench, the willow-pin warm in his hand.

They met first in the garden as they had the week before and the week before that—Elys slipping down the narrow stair from her chamber in the hour after vespers to sit on the old stone bench, Marta folding herself into the hedge like a knot of shadow while Garr lingered where the yew made a dark pocket. The house gave them its noise: chopping in the kitchens, laughter that was not theirs, the great hall settling into its long appetite.

The willow-pin was in Garr's palm from the last time they'd touched it, small and warm. He watched Elys across the bench as if the space between them were a measured thing that could be kept tidy. Marta's eyes flicked to the corridor and then back; when a serving girl passed, Marta tripped her with a smile and a question; the sweep was delayed, the corridor quieted.

"Take it, Garr," Elys said, the line as private as a coin counted in the dark, and he closed his hand around the ivory as if she had lent him a piece of herself.

They spoke in the geography of what was possible and what was not. "They mean to call him Aldric," Elys said, watching his face. "They say Lord Harrow is pleased. He said at table—'Aldric brings Westbrook's levies and a fine marriage with no scandal.'"

Garr's mouth thinned. "Westbrook's levies won't carry my name anywhere but a ledger. I know the back lanes, the river and the mill. I can take a horse and hide a head behind a plough. But I am not the sort to promise more than bread."

Marta leaned nearer, voice dropped to a fretted practicalness. "You have a narrow hour after vespers when the house is noisy and a good fence in the east hedge where the ground dips. I can leave the west shutters unlatched and tell Jory the pantry is missing a tray. I will not be an accomplice in a sermon, but I will put you outside the notice of men who count names." Her hands smoothed the hem of her apron as she spoke; the action was small comfort and small treason.

Later, when the corridor had quieted and the serving girls had been shepherded back, Elys climbed the narrow stairs and stood on the west balcony for a quieter breath. The wood smelled faintly of cut herbs and the far smoke of the kitchens; below, Garr waited where the hedge made its pocket of dark.

"Your hands are cold," Garr said when she leaned on the rail. He lifted his palm and let her fingers rest against the willow's carved leaves.

They did not speak of routes as if hope were a map to be measured—only of what Garr could do, plain as a working man's chores. "Then if we go," he said, steadying the word, "we go on what I can promise. I'll write. I'll fold a note and seal it honest with wax. If I put it where only I can find it, you'll know I mean it."

He drew a scrap of paper from his pouch and with a coin pressed a warm blob of wax to the corner. The fold closed like a small decision. He slipped the sealed scrap beneath his tunic and laid a hand over it.

"I'll write it tonight," he said. The sentence felt like a ladder rung offered to a hand.

Elys stood a moment longer on the balcony watching him below, tracing the willow's tiny carved leaves with her fingertip. Then she turned and went down the stairs again, the wood beneath her feet a practiced sound, and returned to the bench where Garr waited. The garden folded them both back into its hush: Marta to her shadow by the hedge, Garr with the willow-pin like a private law in his palm, the letter warm against his chest. The house settled; the east hedge kept its dark. In the pocket under his tunic the sealed scrap waited, patient as a thing that must be kept alive until needed.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given.     penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.

- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.

- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.

- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.

- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.

thing to do.

the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —

points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

They met first in the garden as they had the week before and the week before that—Elys slipping down the narrow stair from her chamber in the hour after vespers to sit on the old stone bench, Marta folding herself into the hedge like a knot of shadow while Garr lingered where the yew made a dark pocket. The house gave them its noise: chopping in the kitchens, laughter that was not theirs, the great hall settling into its long appetite.

The willow-pin was in Garr's palm from the last time they'd touched it, small and warm. He watched Elys across the bench as if the space between them were a measured thing that could be kept tidy. Marta's eyes flicked to the corridor and then back; when a serving girl passed, Marta tripped her with a smile and a question; the sweep was delayed, the corridor quieted.

"Take it, Garr," Elys said, the line as private as a coin counted in the dark, and he closed his hand around the ivory as if she had lent him a piece of herself.

They spoke in the geography of what was possible and what was not. "They mean to call him Aldric," Elys said, watching his face. "They say Lord Harrow is pleased. He said at table—'Aldric brings Westbrook's levies and a fine marriage with no scandal.'"

Garr's mouth thinned. "Westbrook's levies won't carry my name anywhere but a ledger. I know the back lanes, the river and the mill. I can take a horse and hide a head behind a plough. But I am not the sort to promise more than bread."

Marta leaned nearer, voice dropped to a fretted practicalness. "You have a narrow hour after vespers when the house is noisy and a good fence in the east hedge where the ground dips. I can leave the west shutters unlatched and tell Jory the pantry is missing a tray. I will not be an accomplice in a sermon, but I will put you outside the notice of men who count names." Her hands smoothed the hem of her apron as she spoke; the action was small comfort and small treason.

Later, when the corridor had quieted and the serving girls had been shepherded back, Elys climbed the narrow stairs and stood on the west balcony for a quieter breath. The wood smelled faintly of cut herbs and the far smoke of the kitchens; below, Garr waited where the hedge made its pocket of dark.

"Your hands are cold," Garr said when she leaned on the rail. He lifted his palm and let her fingers rest against the willow's carved leaves.

They did not speak of routes as if hope were a map to be measured—only of what Garr could do, plain as a working man's chores. "Then if we go," he said, steadying the word, "we go on what I can promise. I'll write. I'll fold a note and seal it honest with wax. If I put it where only I can find it, you'll know I mean it."

He drew a scrap of paper from his pouch and with a coin pressed a warm blob of wax to the corner. The fold closed like a small decision. He slipped the sealed scrap beneath his tunic and laid a hand over it.

"I'll write it tonight," he said. The sentence felt like a ladder rung offered to a hand.

Elys stood a moment longer on the balcony watching him below, tracing the willow's tiny carved leaves with her fingertip. Then she turned and went down the stairs again, the wood beneath her feet a practiced sound, and returned to the bench where Garr waited. The garden folded them both back into its hush: Marta to her shadow by the hedge, Garr with the willow-pin like a private law in his palm, the letter warm against his chest. The house settled; the east hedge kept its dark. In the pocket under his tunic the sealed scrap waited, patient as a thing that must be kept alive until needed.

The great hall smelled of rushes and roasted meat and the bright scraping of forks on wood. At the high dais Lord Harrow sat like a careful sentence, and when the hall quieted he let it be known in the way that made conversation fold into obedience.

"Aldric brings Westbrook's levies and a fine marriage with no scandal," he announced, and the words rolled across the benches like a struck bell. Aldric stood by the dais—neat-booted, practiced in the art of polite distance—accepting congratulations with a measured bow. Around the hall faces bloomed into smiles that were both sincere and required; Elys felt the room press at her shoulders as if a cloak had been tightened.

Applause clapped like trapped birds. Elys's hands were clamshells in her lap; she did not look at Aldric. Marta watched from the servants' aisle, her mouth a fold of something that did not quite fit the expression called for above her station.

Outside, beneath the eaves, Garr moved with the quiet efficiency of a man packing what must be carried and leaving what cannot. He had the sealed scrap beneath his tunic—warm against his chest, the wax pressed to a corner—where he'd tucked it for safe keeping. He ran a hand over the leather as if the paper itself might be soothed.

A whisperless stir came from the doorway: Captain Rowan, with two men at his back, had been sent to make a routine check of the yard. Stage direction: Lord Harrow's steward, having noticed hurried movement among the stables after the announcement, sent Rowan to the stables to ensure everything was in order. Rowan's duty, and the household's unease, collided in the doorway.

Rowan's voice was low when he stepped forward to Garr. "We are checking the yard," he said. His eyes flicked to Marta, who had been tending a tray nearby. "Marta—fetch Garr's tunic. Bring it here."

She looked as if someone had wound the air too tight around her ribs. In a voice that was both a confession and a plea, she answered, "I kept their hour like a prayer; they have asked me to unmake that prayer." Her hand trembled as she moved toward the tack-room. The line was a thing dropped between them; it named both what she had protected and the small treason she now performed.

Marta returned with the tunic and handed it over with fingers that would not meet Rowan's face. One of the men ripped at a seam, and a scrap of paper tumbled into his palm—folded, stained at the corner with wax. Rowan took it as if it were a verdict.

He broke the seal with his thumb and read. The hall's din seemed to shrink; the paper's meaning made a private road between him and the dais. He turned, the words gone from his mouth but the command ready.

Lord Harrow read what was shown to him. The lord's face did not flame; it set. He lifted the scrap and the wax between his fingers as evidence, and his voice when he spoke carried the weight of household law.

"This is enough," he said. "Captain Rowan—see that Garr is brought here. Take him from the yard to the courtyard. Let none hinder you."

Rowan folded and held the order like a thing he would answer. For a single beat, his hand hovered at the pommel of the door as if he could choose a different path. Then he exhaled, the sound small and private. "Orders are weights I carry, Lord; they do not make the carrying easy," he said, and his words were apology and oath braided into one.

Two guards moved quickly. Garr, still near the stables, heard the call and braced, but he did not flee—there was nowhere to go without dragging more ruin. Marta watched him with an expression that mixed rescue and remorse; her hands were empty where they had once smoothed a cuff.

The men took Garr by the arms with a practiced surety and threaded him through the servants' passages into the courtyard. The household watched as if watching a lesson. Elys, who had been told of nothing but fate, felt the world narrow to the sight of Garr's back as he was led away.

In the courtyard the air tasted of cold stone and the horse-heat that lingered in the stable doors. Garr's wrists were not yet bound, but the distance he had imagined between himself and the future had been shortened to a measured step toward the dais. The sealed scrap had been placed on the steward's table; a guard kept watch like a small, bright accusation.

Marta stood where she had been made to stand and pressed her palms together as if to still them. She had kept their hour; she had unmade it. The hall resumed its long appetite and Lord Harrow's voice—the voice that rearranged names and marriages—went on with the business of congratulations and duty. Garr was taken toward judgment.

They met first in the garden as they had the week before and the week before that—Elys slipping down the narrow stair from her chamber in the hour after vespers to sit on the old stone bench, Marta folding herself into the hedge like a knot of shadow while Garr lingered where the yew made a dark pocket. The house gave them its noise: chopping in the kitchens, laughter that was not theirs, the great hall settling into its long appetite.

The willow-pin was in Garr's palm from the last time they'd touched it, small and warm. He watched Elys across the bench as if the space between them were a measured thing that could be kept tidy. Marta's eyes flicked to the corridor and then back; when a serving girl passed, Marta tripped her with a smile and a question; the sweep was delayed, the corridor quieted.

"Take it, Garr," Elys said, the line as private as a coin counted in the dark, and he closed his hand around the ivory as if she had lent him a piece of herself.

They spoke in the geography of what was possible and what was not. "They mean to call him Aldric," Elys said, watching his face. "They say Lord Harrow is pleased. He said at table—'Aldric brings Westbrook's levies and a fine marriage with no scandal.'"

Garr's mouth thinned. "Westbrook's levies won't carry my name anywhere but a ledger. I know the back lanes, the river and the mill. I can take a horse and hide a head behind a plough. But I am not the sort to promise more than bread."

Marta leaned nearer, voice dropped to a fretted practicalness. "You have a narrow hour after vespers when the house is noisy and a good fence in the east hedge where the ground dips. I can leave the west shutters unlatched and tell Jory the pantry is missing a tray. I will not be an accomplice in a sermon, but I will put you outside the notice of men who count names." Her hands smoothed the hem of her apron as she spoke; the action was small comfort and small treason.

Later, when the corridor had quieted and the serving girls had been shepherded back, Elys climbed the narrow stairs and stood on the west balcony for a quieter breath. The wood smelled faintly of cut herbs and the far smoke of the kitchens; below, Garr waited where the hedge made its pocket of dark.

"Your hands are cold," Garr said when she leaned on the rail. He lifted his palm and let her fingers rest against the willow's carved leaves.

They did not speak of routes as if hope were a map to be measured—only of what Garr could do, plain as a working man's chores. "Then if we go," he said, steadying the word, "we go on what I can promise. I'll write. I'll fold a note and seal it honest with wax. If I put it where only I can find it, you'll know I mean it."

He drew a scrap of paper from his pouch and with a coin pressed a warm blob of wax to the corner. The fold closed like a small decision. He slipped the sealed scrap beneath his tunic and laid a hand over it.

"I'll write it tonight," he said. The sentence felt like a ladder rung offered to a hand.

Elys stood a moment longer on the balcony watching him below, tracing the willow's tiny carved leaves with her fingertip. Then she turned and went down the stairs again, the wood beneath her feet a practiced sound, and returned to the bench where Garr waited. The garden folded them both back into its hush: Marta to her shadow by the hedge, Garr with the willow-pin like a private law in his palm, the letter warm against his chest. The house settled; the east hedge kept its dark. In the pocket under his tunic the sealed scrap waited, patient as a thing that must be kept alive until needed.

The great hall smelled of rushes and roasted meat and the bright scraping of forks on wood. At the high dais Lord Harrow sat like a careful sentence, and when the hall quieted he let it be known in the way that made conversation fold into obedience.

"Aldric brings Westbrook's levies and a fine marriage with no scandal," he announced, and the words rolled across the benches like a struck bell. Aldric stood by the dais—neat-booted, practiced in the art of polite distance—accepting congratulations with a measured bow. Around the hall faces bloomed into smiles that were both sincere and required; Elys felt the room press at her shoulders as if a cloak had been tightened.

Applause clapped like trapped birds. Elys's hands were clamshells in her lap; she did not look at Aldric. Marta watched from the servants' aisle, her mouth a fold of something that did not quite fit the expression called for above her station.

Outside, beneath the eaves, Garr moved with the quiet efficiency of a man packing what must be carried and leaving what cannot. He had the sealed scrap beneath his tunic—warm against his chest, the wax pressed to a corner—where he'd tucked it for safe keeping. He ran a hand over the leather as if the paper itself might be soothed.

A whisperless stir came from the doorway: Captain Rowan, with two men at his back, had been sent to make a routine check of the yard. Stage direction: Lord Harrow's steward, having noticed hurried movement among the stables after the announcement, sent Rowan to the stables to ensure everything was in order. Rowan's duty, and the household's unease, collided in the doorway.

Rowan's voice was low when he stepped forward to Garr. "We are checking the yard," he said. His eyes flicked to Marta, who had been tending a tray nearby. "Marta—fetch Garr's tunic. Bring it here."

She looked as if someone had wound the air too tight around her ribs. In a voice that was both a confession and a plea, she answered, "I kept their hour like a prayer; they have asked me to unmake that prayer." Her hand trembled as she moved toward the tack-room. The line was a thing dropped between them; it named both what she had protected and the small treason she now performed.

Marta returned with the tunic and handed it over with fingers that would not meet Rowan's face. One of the men ripped at a seam, and a scrap of paper tumbled into his palm—folded, stained at the corner with wax. Rowan took it as if it were a verdict.

He broke the seal with his thumb and read. The hall's din seemed to shrink; the paper's meaning made a private road between him and the dais. He turned, the words gone from his mouth but the command ready.

Lord Harrow read what was shown to him. The lord's face did not flame; it set. He lifted the scrap and the wax between his fingers as evidence, and his voice when he spoke carried the weight of household law.

"This is enough," he said. "Captain Rowan—see that Garr is brought here. Take him from the yard to the courtyard. Let none hinder you."

Rowan folded and held the order like a thing he would answer. For a single beat, his hand hovered at the pommel of the door as if he could choose a different path. Then he exhaled, the sound small and private. "Orders are weights I carry, Lord; they do not make the carrying easy," he said, and his words were apology and oath braided into one.

Two guards moved quickly. Garr, still near the stables, heard the call and braced, but he did not flee—there was nowhere to go without dragging more ruin. Marta watched him with an expression that mixed rescue and remorse; her hands were empty where they had once smoothed a cuff.

The men took Garr by the arms with a practiced surety and threaded him through the servants' passages into the courtyard. The household watched as if watching a lesson. Elys, who had been told of nothing but fate, felt the world narrow to the sight of Garr's back as he was led away.

In the courtyard the air tasted of cold stone and the horse-heat that lingered in the stable doors. Garr's wrists were not yet bound, but the distance he had imagined between himself and the future had been shortened to a measured step toward the dais. The courtyard smelled of cold stone and horse-heat and the kind of silence that sits before something is done. The dais they built for punishment stood plain against the sky, a beam and a ladder and the small practiced platform where decisions were made visible. Guards ringed it like an obedience; a crowd that had been household and feast gathered now as if to learn what order looked like when it took breath.

Elys pushed through the press with Marta at her elbow, breath sharp as a bell. She had not been told—no summons had been given to her—but the sight of Garr in the centre, pale against the paving and held by two men, drew the whole of her into a single, tearless moment. His hands were empty; the willow-pin was gone from his palm. He saw her and his face did something like a question.

Lord Harrow stood above them on the steps, his shape cut by the long line of the house's will. He did not shout. He made a small motion of the hand and the manager of the steward's household read the sentence as if from a dry ledger.

"For conspiracy and the aiding of escape," the steward said, "the sentence of this household is death by hanging."

Garr's shoulders did not shrink from the words. He had the slow steadiness of a man who had known his edges for years. Elys moved as if drawn by a thread and slipped a hand into her sleeve—Marta's eyes widened—and produced the little ivory willow-pin. She crossed the space to him with a child's quickness and pressed it into his palm.

"Take it, Garr," she said, the words clean and quiet as they had been nights ago. He closed his fingers around the pin, and for a heartbeat they held each other's hands the way people hold a thing that's all there is to hold.

Rowan stood nearest the platform, the order in his hand like a brand. When Lord Harrow nodded, Rowan gave the signal with the same professional calm that had become part of his skin. He turned, and for a second his jaw trembled as if with something like the memory of a kindness he had once given.

"Orders are weights I carry, Lord; they do not make the carrying easy," he said, aloud though it was meant as a small excuse to himself.

The execution was swift. The rope took Garr with a single, terrible explanation; he swung once on the beam and then was still. A curdle of sound went through the watching people—a sound that was not cheering and not mourning, only the acknowledgment of a thing concluded.

Elys bent as if to touch his boots and then, as if a plan made itself, climbed the ladder with the speed of someone who would not be denied a conclusion. She pressed the willow-pin to his lips and kissed it, and then, without a word, she looped the rope over her own head.

Marta's hand went to her mouth and she cried out—one small, animal sound—and tried to take her. Hands reached; guards hesitated as if even they felt the wrongness of catching a lord's daughter. Elys's feet left the platform. The air closed around her as it had closed around Garr, and she went where he had gone.

They were dead. The steward closed his book and the hush spread like a cloth over the courtyard. Lord Harrow's face did not fall into triumph; it was the flat, exhausted line of a man who had paid a bill he thought would settle favor and found only more accounts.

Marta stooped after the crowd had been pushed back. She picked the little willow-pin from the dust where it had fallen and folded it into her palm as if it were something that might still be kept from being broken. She pressed it to her breast, a gesture that was not comfort but accusation.

Rowan stood with his head lowered. Later he would say what he had said here in smaller voice: that he had answered an order; that the weight would remain. For now his stillness said what a single line could not.

The household dispersed with slow, mechanical care. Aldric watched from the house's shadow, expression set. Lord Harrow went back into the hall as if to close a ledger. His victory was a silence that filled up rooms: practical, uncelebratory. The courtyard kept the shape of two bodies on the paving and the small, stubborn presence of a willow carved in ivory on the stone where Marta still held it.

Marta folded her hands over the pin and whispered to herself the line she had already spoken in a corridor and could not take back. "I kept their hour like a prayer; they have asked me to unmake that prayer."

What had been private was now evidence; what had been love was now a lesson. The house returned to its tasks, but many of its faces had been rearranged by what they had seen.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one

brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair

scored.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. In the scuffle a guard's gloved hand brushed Garr's palm and something small and bright clinked free; Marta's fingers were there before anyone noticed, and without a sound she caught the ivory and slipped it into Elys's sleeve as the girl surged forward.

His hands were empty; the willow-pin was gone from his palm. He saw her and his face did something like a question.

Lord Harrow stood above them on the steps, his shape cut by the long line of the house's will. He did not shout. He made a small motion of the hand and the manager of the steward's household read the sentence as if from a dry ledger.

"For conspiracy and the aiding of escape," the steward said, "the sentence of this household is death by hanging."

Garr's shoulders did not shrink from the words. He had the slow steadiness of a man who had known his edges for years. Elys moved as if drawn by a thread and produced the little ivory willow-pin from her sleeve. She crossed the space to him with a child's quickness and pressed it into his palm.

"Take it, Garr," she said, the words clean and quiet as they had been nights ago. He closed his fingers around the pin, and for a heartbeat they held each other's hands the way people hold a thing that's all there is to hold.

Rowan stood nearest the platform, the order in his hand like a brand. When Lord Harrow nodded, Rowan gave the signal with the same professional calm that had become part of his skin. He turned, and for a second his jaw trembled as if with something like the memory of a kindness he had once given.

"Orders are weights I carry, Lord; they do not make the carrying easy," he said, aloud though it was meant as a small excuse to himself.

The execution was swift. The rope took Garr with a single, terrible explanation; he swung once on the beam and then was still. A curdle of sound went through the watching people—a sound that was not cheering and not mourning, only the acknowledgment of a thing concluded.

Elys bent as if to touch his boots and then, as if a plan made itself, climbed the ladder with the speed of someone who would not be denied a conclusion. She pressed the willow-pin to his lips and kissed it, and then, without a word, she looped the rope over her own head.

Marta's hand went to her mouth and she cried out—one small, animal sound—and tried to take her. Hands reached; guards hesitated as if even they felt the wrongness of catching a lord's daughter. Elys's feet left the platform. The air closed around her as it had closed around Garr, and she went where he had gone.

They were dead. The steward closed his book and the hush spread like a cloth over the courtyard. Lord Harrow's face did not fall into triumph; it was the flat, exhausted line of a man who had paid a bill he thought would settle favor and found only more accounts.

When the crowd had been pushed back Marta stooped and found the little willow-pin where it had fallen and folded it into her palm as if it were something that might still be kept from being broken. She pressed it to her breast, a gesture that was not comfort but accusation.

Rowan stood with his head lowered. Later he would say what he had said here in smaller voice: that he had answered an order; that the weight would remain. For now his stillness said what a single line could not.

The household dispersed with slow, mechanical care. Aldric watched from the house's shadow, expression set. Lord Harrow went back into the hall as if to close a ledger. His victory was a silence that filled up rooms: practical, uncelebratory. The courtyard kept the shape of two bodies on the paving and the small, stubborn presence of a willow carved in ivory on the stone where Marta still held it.

Marta folded her hands over the pin and whispered to herself the line she had already spoken in a corridor and could not take back. "I kept their hour like a prayer; they have asked me to unmake that prayer." 

What had been private was now evidence; what had been love was now a lesson. The house returned to its tasks, but many of its faces had been rearranged by what they had seen.
